name: Schooner Drift
geological_features: Continent-sized ice floes drifting on a subsurface liquid water ocean
Ice cliffs hundreds of meters high where floes collide
description: Schooner Drift is a small ice world whose frozen surface is not a single continuous shell but a collection of continent-sized ice floes drifting on a subsurface ocean of liquid water maintained by tidal heating. The floes move with geological patience, their progress measurable only over years, but where they meet, they produce ice cliffs of staggering scale — walls of compressed ice hundreds of meters high, groaning and cracking as the plates grind against each other.

The thin atmosphere carries the sound of the ice — a constant symphony of creaks, pops, and deep bass groans as the floes shift and settle. Cryogeysers erupt along the floe margins where subsurface water finds pathways to the surface, their plumes of ice crystals catching the distant starlight in brief, glittering displays. The cold is profound and penetrating, the kind that finds every gap in insulation and punishes any exposed surface.

The drifting floes follow patterns that have been mapped over decades of observation, their movements influenced by the subsurface ocean currents driven by tidal forces from the parent gas giant. Some floes have completed full circumnavigations of the planet, a journey taking approximately three hundred standard years. Navigation markers placed on the ice by early survey teams have been tracked as they drift, providing invaluable data on both surface and subsurface dynamics.

Schooner Drift's subsurface ocean represents a significant water reserve in a system otherwise poor in accessible volatiles, and ice-mining operations extract water from the floe margins where the ice is newest and least contaminated. The operations must relocate periodically as the floes drift, giving the mining camps a nomadic character that their crews have embraced with surprising enthusiasm. Life on a drifting ice world, they say, teaches patience.
